mouth.name: Mouth
mouth.what: Teeth cut and grind food while the tongue mixes it with saliva into a soft ball called a bolus.
mouth.chemistry: Salivary amylase starts breaking starch into smaller sugars. Lingual lipase begins on fat, but very little happens yet.
mouth.fact: Your salivary glands make roughly 1 to 1.5 litres of saliva a day.

esophagus.name: Food pipe (oesophagus)
esophagus.what: Waves of muscle contraction, called peristalsis, push each swallow down to the stomach in a few seconds.
esophagus.chemistry: No digestion happens here. Mucus helps the bolus slide.
esophagus.fact: Peristalsis works even upside down — astronauts can swallow in space.

stomach.name: Stomach
stomach.what: The stomach stores the meal, churns it with acid into a thick liquid called chyme, and lets it out a little at a time through the pyloric sphincter.
stomach.chemistry: Hydrochloric acid unfolds proteins and kills many microbes. Pepsin starts cutting proteins into shorter chains. Liquids leave first; solids must be ground to tiny pieces before they can leave.
stomach.absorbed: Very little — some water, alcohol and a few drugs.
stomach.fact: The more calories a meal has, the more slowly it leaves: the small intestine signals the stomach to deliver only a few calories per minute.

smallIntestine.name: Small intestine
smallIntestine.what: Chyme moves through about 3 metres of narrow tube. Its lining is folded into millions of villi that give it a huge surface for absorption.
smallIntestine.chemistry: Bile from the liver breaks fat into tiny droplets. Pancreatic enzymes — amylase, lipase, trypsin — and enzymes on the villi finish breaking food into sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol.
smallIntestine.absorbed: Most nutrients and most of the water are absorbed here into the blood and lymph.
smallIntestine.fact: The villi and microvilli give the small intestine a surface area of around 30 square metres — about half a badminton court (Helander and Fändriks, 2014).

largeIntestine.name: Large intestine
largeIntestine.what: What could not be digested — mainly fibre — moves slowly through the colon and is stored until it leaves the body.
largeIntestine.chemistry: Gut bacteria ferment fibre, making gases and short-chain fatty acids that feed the colon’s own cells. Some vitamins, such as vitamin K, are made by bacteria here.
largeIntestine.absorbed: Most of the remaining water and salts.
largeIntestine.fact: This is the slowest part of the journey: commonly a day or more.

flagship.setup: Two rotis with a glass of water at 0 h, and a 20-minute walk from 1 h. Kept to compare: the same meal, resting.
flagship.book: NCERT Class 10: digested food is absorbed in the small intestine, and blood carries it around the body.

tasks.q: At 30 min, where is the roti, and what has started to rise in the blood?
tasks.b: NCERT Class 10: digested food is absorbed in the small intestine.
tasks.m: The roti leaves the stomach a little at a time; blood sugar has started to rise.

tasks.q: Sketch breaths a minute from 0 to 3 h, with the walk and without. How many breaths a minute during the walk, and without it?
tasks.b: Older NCERT Class 7 book (2024-25): 15–18 a minute at rest.
tasks.m: About 24 a minute in the walk, about 16 without it.

tasks.q: How fast does the heart beat during the walk, and without it?
tasks.b: Older NCERT Class 7 book (2024-25): 72–80 beats a minute at rest.
tasks.m: About 94 a minute in the walk, about 67 without it.

tasks.q: Where does the water from the glass go? Does more or less come out after the walk?
tasks.b: NCERT Class 10: the kidneys filter about 180 L a day, and only a litre or two leaves as urine.
tasks.m: It leaves as urine. By 1 h 51 min about 60 mL less has come out than without the walk: sweat took some water.

exit.q: Which system hardly changed after the roti, but changed a lot during the walk?
exit.m: Breathing: about 16 breaths a minute after the roti, about 24 during the walk.

stomachRace.setup: One cola at 0 h. Kept to compare: a cheeseburger with fries.
stomachRace.book: NCERT Class 10: a muscle at the end of the stomach lets food into the small intestine in small amounts.

tasks.q: When has half of the cola left the stomach?
tasks.m: About 35 min (30 to 40 is right).

tasks.q: Sketch the food in the stomach from 0 to 6 h for both meals. Mark where each line is half way down.
tasks.m: The cola’s line falls at once and is half way down at about 35 min; the burger and fries fall slowly, half way at about 4 h 35 min.

tasks.q: Which leaves the stomach faster, and why?
tasks.m: The cola, about 8 times faster: a drink starts leaving straight away, and it has fewer calories than a burger with fries.

tasks.q: What is blood sugar 1 hour after the cola?
tasks.m: About 111 mg/dL (105 to 115). Its highest, about 121, was at 35 min.

exit.q: In which part of the gut is most digested food absorbed?

rotiDal.setup: Roti with dal at 0 h. Kept to compare: white rice.
rotiDal.book: NCERT Class 10: digested food is absorbed in the small intestine, and blood carries it around the body.

tasks.q: What is the highest blood sugar after roti and dal, and when?
tasks.m: About 110 mg/dL, at about 1 h 6 min.

tasks.q: What is the highest blood sugar after white rice, and when?
tasks.m: About 124 mg/dL, at about 57 min.

tasks.q: Sketch blood sugar from 0 to 4 h for both meals. Which line rises more gently?
tasks.m: Roti and dal: its highest point is lower, and it comes later.

tasks.q: Before eating, blood sugar is about 90 mg/dL. How far above that does each meal take it at most?
tasks.m: Roti and dal about 20 mg/dL above it, white rice about 34 mg/dL above it.

exit.q: Which meal gives the slower, gentler rise in blood sugar, and how can you tell from the graph?
exit.m: Roti and dal: its line rises more slowly, and its highest point is lower.

colaFour.setup: One cola at 0 h. Kept to compare: four colas at once.
colaFour.book: NCERT Class 10: digested food is absorbed in the small intestine, and blood carries it around the body.

tasks.q: What is the highest blood sugar after one cola, and after four?
tasks.m: About 121 mg/dL for both, at about 35 min.

tasks.q: At 2 h, what is blood sugar after one cola, and after four?
tasks.m: About 91 mg/dL after one, about 103 mg/dL after four.

tasks.q: Sketch blood sugar from 0 to 6 h for one cola and for four. Which line stays raised longer?
tasks.m: Four colas: blood sugar stays raised about 3 h 15 min longer.

tasks.q: When has half of the drink left the stomach: one cola, and four?
tasks.m: About 35 min for one, about 2 h 15 min for four.

exit.q: Four colas did not take blood sugar higher than one. What did they change?
exit.m: How long it stays raised: about 3 h 15 min longer.

breathRun.setup: Two rotis at 0 h, and a 10-minute run from 30 min. Kept to compare: the same meal, resting.
breathRun.book: Older NCERT Class 7 book (2024-25): 15–18 breaths a minute for a grown-up at rest, up to 25 a minute in heavy exercise.

tasks.q: How many breaths a minute at rest?
tasks.b: Older NCERT Class 7 book (2024-25): 15–18 a minute.
tasks.m: 15 a minute, for one resting grown-up.

tasks.q: How many breaths a minute at the end of the run?
tasks.b: Older NCERT Class 7 book: up to 25 a minute in heavy exercise.
tasks.m: About 33 a minute: the model follows grown-ups running hard.

tasks.q: How much air goes in with each breath at rest, and in the run?
tasks.m: About 0.4 L at rest, about 1.4 L in the run.

tasks.q: Sketch breaths a minute from 0 to 2 h, running and resting. When is the line highest?
tasks.m: At the end of the run (40 min), about 33 a minute; soon after, back near 15.

exit.q: Why do you breathe faster and deeper when you run?
exit.b: Older NCERT Class 7 book (2024-25): when we exercise we breathe fast and take deep breaths, and so take in more oxygen.
exit.m: Breathing brings the oxygen in and carries the carbon dioxide away: in the run the body uses about 10 times as much oxygen as at rest.

heartWalk.setup: Roti with dal at 0 h, and a 20-minute walk from 1 h. Kept to compare: the same meal, resting.
heartWalk.book: NCERT Class 10: blood carries digested food and oxygen around the body, and it goes through the heart twice in each round.
heartWalk.y: Blood to the gut (mL a minute)

tasks.q: How many times a minute does the heart beat at rest?
tasks.b: Older NCERT Class 7 book (2024-25): 72–80 beats a minute.
tasks.m: About 66 a minute, for one resting grown-up.

tasks.q: How many times a minute does it beat in the walk?
tasks.m: About 93 a minute at 1 h 10 min.

tasks.q: How much blood goes to the muscles each minute at rest, and in the walk?
tasks.m: About 0.9 L at rest, about 4.3 L in the walk.

tasks.q: Sketch the blood going to the gut from 0 to 4 h, resting. When does the most blood go to the gut?
tasks.m: About 1 h after eating, while the small intestine takes in the food.

exit.q: In one round of the body, how many times does blood go through the heart?

drinkWater.setup: Four glasses of water at 0 h. Kept to compare: one glass.
drinkWater.book: NCERT Class 10: the kidneys filter about 180 L a day, and only a litre or two leaves as urine.

tasks.q: Sketch the urine made per hour from 0 to 4 h, for four glasses and for one. When is it fastest?
tasks.m: About 1 h after drinking, for both.

tasks.q: At the most, how much urine is made in an hour after four glasses, and after one?
tasks.m: About 700 mL an hour after four, about 220 mL an hour after one.

tasks.q: How much do the kidneys filter, and how much of it leaves?
tasks.b: NCERT Class 10: about 180 L a day; only a litre or two leaves as urine.
tasks.k: About 125 mL a minute (OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e).

tasks.q: Is there glucose in the urine?
tasks.k: None: the kidneys take all of it back.

exit.q: What happens to the water from the three extra glasses?
exit.b: NCERT Class 10: how much water is taken back depends on how much extra water there is in the body.
exit.m: By 4 h about 670 mL more urine has come out than after one glass.

fatRoad.setup: A cheeseburger with fries at 0 h. Kept to compare: two rotis.
fatRoad.book: NCERT Class 10: lymph carries digested and absorbed fat from the intestine, and drains extra fluid back into the blood.

tasks.q: Which road does fat from the intestine take to the blood?
tasks.b: NCERT Class 10: lymph carries digested and absorbed fat from the intestine.
tasks.m: Into lymph vessels, up the main lymph duct, into a vein in the neck.

tasks.q: Sketch blood fat from 0 to 12 h, for the cheeseburger with fries and for the rotis. How high does each go?
tasks.m: About 101 mg/dL with the cheeseburger and fries, and it stays up for hours; about 86 mg/dL with the rotis (80 before eating).

tasks.q: Does the sugar from the meal take the same road?
tasks.m: No. In this model sugar goes from the intestine straight into the blood; only fat goes by lymph.

tasks.q: What other job does lymph do?
tasks.b: NCERT Class 10: it drains extra fluid from the spaces between cells back into the blood.
tasks.k: About 3 L of tissue fluid a day (OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e).

exit.q: Why does blood fat stay up for hours after the cheeseburger with fries, but not after the rotis?
exit.m: The cheeseburger and fries have about 32 g of fat and leave the stomach slowly, so fat keeps arriving by lymph for hours; the rotis have about 3 g.

musclesRun.setup: Two rotis at 0 h, and a 10-minute run from 30 min. Kept to compare: the same meal, resting.
musclesRun.book: NCERT Class 10: food is used in cells to provide energy; with oxygen, glucose is broken down completely into carbon dioxide and water.

tasks.q: How many times their resting energy do the muscles use in the run?
tasks.m: About 43 times.

tasks.q: Where does most of that extra energy end up?
tasks.m: As heat; sweat carries it away.

tasks.q: How fast does the heart beat in the run, and how many breaths a minute?
tasks.m: About 160 beats and about 33 breaths a minute.

tasks.q: Sketch the muscles’ energy from 0 to 2 h, running and resting. When is it highest?
tasks.m: In the run (30 to 40 min); before and after, it stays at the resting level.

exit.q: Which other body systems change when the muscles work harder?
exit.m: Breathing, the heart and the skin: faster breaths, a faster heart, and sweat.

sweatRun.setup: Two rotis at 0 h, and a 10-minute run from 30 min. Kept to compare: the same meal, resting.
sweatRun.book: NCERT Class 6: the normal temperature of a healthy human body is taken to be 37.0 °C.

tasks.q: How much sweat is made in the run, and resting?
tasks.m: About 170 mL in all; none from moving when resting.

tasks.q: What happens to body temperature?
tasks.b: NCERT Class 6: normal body temperature is taken to be 37.0 °C.
tasks.m: Held at 37 °C: the model does not work it out. Sweat takes the extra heat away.

tasks.q: Is sweat fat leaving the body?
tasks.m: No: sweat is water and salt, not fat leaving.

tasks.q: Sketch the sweat made per hour from 0 to 2 h, running and resting. When is it highest?
tasks.m: At the end of the run (40 min), about 980 mL an hour; none at rest.

exit.q: Where does the extra energy of running go, and how does the body get rid of it?
exit.m: Most of it becomes heat; sweat carries the heat away.

insulinCola.setup: A glass of cola at 0 h. Kept to compare: a glass of water.
insulinCola.book: NCERT Class 10 (Ch 6, p. 111): when blood sugar rises, the pancreas makes more insulin; as it falls, less.

tasks.q: Sketch insulin from 0 to 4 h, after the cola and after the water. When is it highest?
tasks.m: About 25 min after the cola, at about 7.3× before eating; with the water it stays at 1×.

tasks.q: What is insulin’s job?
tasks.b: NCERT Class 10 (Ch 6, pp. 110–111): it helps to regulate blood sugar; the pancreas makes more when blood sugar rises (feedback).

tasks.q: Does the brain use more sugar after the cola?
tasks.k: No: about 4.4 g an hour all day (Mergenthaler et al. 2013).

exit.q: Does a walk lower blood sugar in this model?
exit.m: Not yet in this model: moving does not change blood sugar here.

reflexHotPan.setup: The hot-pan demo: the same touch twice, slowed down. ● is the reflex through the spinal cord, ○ the route through the brain. Press “Touch the hot pan”; the counters show the real time.
reflexHotPan.book: NCERT Class 10 (Ch 6, p. 102): reflex arcs have evolved because “the thinking process of the brain is not fast enough”.
reflexHotPan.y: Signal on its way (● reflex, ○ through the brain)

tasks.q: In a reflex, where does the signal pass from the nerve that senses the heat to the nerve that moves the muscle?
tasks.b: NCERT Class 10 (Ch 6, p. 102): in the spinal cord itself; the information also goes on to reach the brain.

tasks.q: Sketch both routes from 0 to 250 ms: mark when the reflex reaches the arm muscle, and when the command through the brain does.
tasks.m: The reflex at about 64 ms; the route through the brain at about 214 ms, about three times as long.

tasks.q: Which part of the reflex takes most of its time?
tasks.k: Heat goes in on a thin fibre at about 15 m/s; the command comes out on a thick one at about 95 m/s (Kiernan 2003).
tasks.m: The way in, from the fingertip to the spinal cord: about 58 of the 64 ms.

tasks.q: Turn on “Myelin off (thin fibres)” (beyond class 10). How long does the reflex take now?
tasks.m: About 883 ms, about 14 times as long. A what-if: real motor nerves always have myelin.

exit.q: Why do you pull your hand back before you have thought about the pain?
exit.b: NCERT Class 10 (Ch 6, p. 102): thinking it all through takes time, too long when we touch a hot object; a reflex arc is quicker.
exit.m: The reflex turns round in the spinal cord and reaches the arm muscle in about 64 ms; thinking adds about 150 ms.

science.title: Science and sources
science.lead: What the model computes, what it assumes, and where every number comes from.
science.modelBody: Stomach emptying is computed from the meal. Drinks start leaving straight away — water within minutes, drinks with calories at about 2 kcal per minute. Solid food is first ground for about 20 minutes, then leaves at about 1.4 kcal per minute, so meals with more calories take longer. (In the model a bigger meal empties at the same rate; real stomachs speed up a little for big meals.) Blood sugar is computed from the carbohydrate being absorbed, its glycemic index, and the slowing effect of fat and protein.
science.fixedBody: Time in the small and large intestine varies far more between people than between meals, so LifePeek uses typical published values and shows the range.
limits: Models a healthy adult only — not children, pregnancy, diabetes or digestive illness.
Blood sugar is a typical shape, not a prediction for any one person.
Exercise, sleep, stress and drinks with the meal all change real results.
Glycemic index values for mixed and home-cooked dishes vary between studies.
Fibre isn't modelled on its own: its slowing effect on blood sugar shows up through each food's glycemic index.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.summary: **Short version: LifePeek does not ask for, collect or store anything about you.** There are no accounts, no logins, no ads, no cookies and no tracking.

sections.title: What stays on your device
intro: LifePeek saves a few things **in your own browser only**. They are never sent to us:
items: your language (English or Hindi), whether Projector mode is on, and whether you have closed the "not medical advice" note;
whether you have chosen less movement on screen (reduced motion);
whether you have switched off the letter-key shortcuts;
a one-time note that the page has just reloaded after an update error (deleted when you close the tab);
a copy of the app, so it works offline in class;
the meals you pick are kept in the page address (the link). A share link contains only the meals, nothing about you.
outro: You can delete all of this by clearing the site data for {{host}} in your browser settings.

sections.title: Reporting a mistake
intro: When you press **Report a mistake**, LifePeek opens a **GitHub issue** in a new tab with your report already filled in. **Nothing is sent to us. Your report text reaches GitHub only inside the link that opens the form, and nothing is published until you press Submit there.** You choose whether to send it.
items: GitHub issues are **public**. Anyone can read them.
You need a GitHub account, and GitHub only allows accounts for people aged 13 and over. If you are younger, ask your teacher to send the report.
GitHub's own privacy statement applies to your account and the issue: https://docs.github.com/site-policy/privacy-policies/github-general-privacy-statement
**Don't type your name, school, phone number, email or any health information** in the report. Just say what is wrong and, if you can, where the right number comes from.
If you posted something by mistake, ask us (see "Contact" below) and we will delete the issue.

sections.title: Hosting
intro: The app is served by Vercel, a web hosting company. Like every website, Vercel's servers see your IP address and browser type when your device downloads the app, and may keep this in logs for a limited time, for security and to keep the site running, under Vercel's privacy policy: https://vercel.com/legal/privacy-policy. We do not use these logs to find out who you are, and we do not combine them with anything else.
items: **Analytics are switched off.** We do not use Vercel Analytics, Google Analytics or any other tracker.
Fonts and pictures are part of the app, so your browser does not contact Google or other services.

The **Stats** page only shows counts of public GitHub issues (mistake reports). We read them from GitHub once a week when the site is built, so on that page your browser does not contact GitHub: it only downloads a small file from this site.

sections.title: How long we keep things
items: **On our side: nothing**, because we don't receive anything about you.
Reports on GitHub stay public until they are deleted. We delete any report that contains personal details as soon as we see it.

If we later add our own report form, we will update this page **before** it goes live. The plan is: no name or email fields, IP addresses used only for a moment to stop spam (never saved), server logs deleted within 14 days, and reports deleted within 90 days after they are handled.

sections.title: Children and India's data protection law
intro: LifePeek is made for school students. India's **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act)** protects personal data, with extra care for children. We follow it by not collecting personal data at all, so there is nothing to ask parents' consent for. If this ever changes, we will update this page first.

outro: Maintainer: {{name}} (GitHub: @Sarthaks-24). We aim to reply within 7 days.

sections.title: Not medical advice
intro: LifePeek is an **educational model of a typical healthy adult**. Times and blood-sugar values are typical ranges and vary a lot between people. **It is not medical advice.** Do not use it to make health, diet or medical decisions. If you have diabetes or any health concern, talk to a doctor.

breathRate.name: Breaths a minute
breathRate.desc: How many times a minute the body breathes in and out. The model works it out from the carbon dioxide the body makes: more work makes more carbon dioxide, and more breaths carry it away.

tidalVolume.name: Air per breath
tidalVolume.desc: How much air goes in with each breath. Harder work makes breaths deeper as well as faster.

o2UseRate.name: Oxygen used
o2UseRate.desc: The oxygen the body takes from the air each minute, worked out from the energy it uses (Weir’s formula).

co2OutRate.name: Carbon dioxide made
co2OutRate.desc: The carbon dioxide the body makes each minute and breathes out.

exchangeRatio.name: Carbon dioxide for each oxygen
exchangeRatio.desc: How much carbon dioxide is made for each unit of oxygen used: about 0.8 at rest, nearer 1 when the body runs mostly on sugar.

rate.name: Heart beats a minute
rate.desc: How many times a minute the heart beats. The model works it out from the blood pumped a minute and the blood pushed out with each beat: more work needs more blood, and the heart beats faster and harder to send it.

output.name: Blood pumped a minute
output.desc: How much blood the heart pumps each minute, in litres. Moving muscles need more oxygen, so the heart pumps more; digesting a meal adds a little.

strokeVolume.name: Blood per beat
strokeVolume.desc: How much blood the heart pushes out with each beat. It grows with activity, like walking or running, up to about 1.4 times, and a little after a meal.

energyRate.name: Energy used by muscles
energyRate.desc: How much energy the muscles use each hour. At rest they use about a fifth of the body’s resting energy, steadily; activity adds all of its extra energy here, and most of it ends up as heat.

sweatRate.name: Sweat made
sweatRate.desc: How much sweat the skin makes each hour. In this model sweat carries away the extra heat of activity, so it comes only with it.

sweatTotal.name: Sweat so far
sweatTotal.desc: All the sweat made since the start of the clock.

urineRate.name: Urine made per hour
urineRate.desc: How much urine the kidneys make each hour. Water from drinks and food makes more for an hour or two; water lost in sweat makes a little less for a while.

urineTotal.name: Urine made so far
urineTotal.desc: All the urine made since the start: a steady day’s, about 1.5 L a day, plus what the meal’s water adds.

bladderMl.name: Urine in the bladder
bladderMl.desc: The urine stored in the bladder. At about 150 mL it starts to feel full; here it empties at 300 mL.

filtrationRate.name: Blood filtered by the kidneys
filtrationRate.desc: How much liquid the kidneys filter out of the blood each minute, about 125 mL. Almost all of it is taken back; only a little leaves as urine.

bodyExtraMl.name: Water in the body above normal
bodyExtraMl.desc: Water from drinks and food that is in the body and has not yet left as urine. Below zero means sweat took more than you drank: the model assumes you drink it back over about 90 minutes.

fatFlowRate.name: Fat reaching the blood by lymph
fatFlowRate.desc: How much of the meal’s fat lymph carries to the blood each minute. Fat taken in by the small intestine goes into lymph vessels first, then up the main lymph duct into a vein in the neck.

glucoseUse.name: Sugar used by the brain
glucoseUse.desc: Sugar (glucose) the brain uses each hour, about the same all day. Between meals the liver keeps it supplied.

limits.glucoseTail: After big, fatty meals the model shows a small, slow tail; real bodies usually settle a little sooner.
limits.glucoseBand: The shaded band is a model estimate of how much healthy people differ.
limits.energyInAtwater: Each gram of carbohydrate or protein counts as 4 kcal and each gram of fat as 9 kcal, so the total can be a little different from the food label. These standard numbers already allow for the bit of food the body cannot take in. The model also counts only what was taken in, so that bit is left out twice and energy coming in reads a few per cent low. The small amount of energy in fibre is not counted.
limits.energyUsedResting: This is a formula for a resting adult (the ICMR-NIN 2020 reference adult, 65 kg), not a measurement. It does not change with the meal.
limits.backToBase: "Back near the before-meal level" means within 5 mg/dL of it.
limits.glucoseSameHighest: More of the same food or drink does not raise the highest point here, only how long blood sugar stays up: the stomach lets food out at a steady rate (about 2 kcal a minute for a sugary drink), whatever the amount. The model leaves out anything else a bigger portion might do to the highest point in real people.
limits.steadyEmptying: The model lets food out of the stomach at a steady rate until it is empty. So after a big meal the food in the stomach falls in a straight line, and blood sugar and energy coming in stay level for hours, then fall within about an hour. Real stomachs usually slow down near the end, so the fall is gentler. After 6 hours the time axis is squeezed (the hatched part on the right), which makes the fall look steeper still.
limits.activityMet: Each activity uses an average value from the 2024 Compendium of Physical Activities for a 65 kg adult. Real people differ with speed, fitness and size. The first 2–3 minutes of extra energy used after stopping are shown; the slower, longer part is not.
limits.foodEffect: The share of energy used to digest each nutrient is a value inside the ranges from studies (carbohydrate 7.5 %, protein 25 %, fat 2 %). It differs between people and meals.
limits.gasExchange: Oxygen used and carbon dioxide made are worked out from the energy the body uses (Weir’s formula, without protein). The air in the lungs is taken to keep the same carbon dioxide, so the blood’s oxygen and carbon dioxide do not change here.
limits.breathSplit: How the extra air is shared between faster and deeper breaths is a rule picked by hand (a model estimate): real people differ.
limits.breathAdult: The numbers are for a typical grown-up. Children usually breathe faster.
limits.heartSplit: How a faster heart is shared between more beats and more blood per beat is a rule from studies of grown-ups (a model estimate); after a meal the share is from one small study. Fitness, posture and age are not in the model, and the rule “220 minus age” is not for children.
limits.heartOutput: Blood pumped a minute is worked out from the oxygen the body uses (about 5.5 litres more blood for each extra litre of oxygen), from small studies of grown-ups. Blood pressure is not worked out: 120/80 is a book value, held.
limits.gutFlow: How much more blood goes to the gut after a meal is fitted to one study of a very big meal, so small drinks barely move it. In hard exercise the gut gives some of its blood to the muscles (OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Table 20.3).
limits.heartAdult: The numbers are for a typical grown-up. Children’s hearts usually beat faster.
limits.heartRecovery: After an activity the model’s heart slows back almost to resting within a few minutes. Real hearts slow quickly at first, then stay a little fast for longer: recovery is simplified here.
limits.heartDrawing: In the drawing the blood’s dashes run at most twice as fast as at rest; in a run the heart really pumps about 3.5 times as much blood. The beat is enlarged to be seen.
limits.muscleEnergy: Resting muscle energy is worked out from studies of how much energy muscle uses and how much of the body is muscle, for a typical 65 kg adult (a model estimate). All the extra energy of activity is counted in the muscles, the heart’s and the breathing muscles’ extra work included.
limits.sweatWarmRoom: The model takes a warm room: all the extra heat of moving leaves as sweat, and sweat starts and stops with the activity. Body temperature is kept within a narrow range, not worked out. Room temperature is not part of this model. Sweat is water and salt, not fat.
limits.waterSteadyDay: We assume a steady day: about 1.5 L of urine a day from other food and drink. The body is always well watered, so sweat is drunk back over about 90 minutes.
limits.bladderEmpties: At about 150 mL the bladder starts to feel full, and we can usually wait. Here it empties at 300 mL; a person chooses when.
limits.gfrFixed: The kidneys filter about 125 mL a minute all day here (90–140 in grown men). This model does not sleep: urine is not slower at night.
limits.waterSimple: The model has no salt: milk and ORS, which the body holds on to a little longer, count the same as plain water. Any drink’s water counts the same. The numbers are for a typical grown man.
limits.lymphFat: All of a meal’s fat goes to the blood by lymph here, about half an hour after the gut takes it in, and the blood clears it in one step. Fat the liver sends out and fat used as fuel are left out. One grown-up.
limits.bloodFatLate: After a big meal of solid food, blood fat peaks later here than in studies (often after 6 h instead of 3–4 h), because food leaves the stomach slowly in this model. Read the hours as rough.
limits.bloodFatIndia: Blood fat before eating is 80 mg/dL here. Many Indian adults start higher: 116 mg/dL on average in the ICMR-INDIAB study (Joshi 2014). People differ.
limits.insulinOpenLoop: Insulin here follows the sugar coming in from food; it does not pull blood sugar back down. Blood sugar is the same line as in Digestion, from studies of real meals, which already include what insulin does.
limits.insulinHigh: Two hours after a 75 g glucose drink (the lab sugar test, not one of the app’s foods), the model’s insulin is higher than in a study (about 9×, where young women measured about 6×: Takahashi 2018), and after a big solid meal it stays raised for hours, because the stomach empties slowly here.
limits.insulinSugarOnly: Only sugar and starch from food raise insulin in this model. In real life protein and fat raise it a little too; here an egg leaves it at 1×.
limits.insulinHealthy: This is a healthy body that makes its own insulin. In diabetes (madhumeh) the body makes too little insulin or its cells answer it less; this model does not show that, and a family glucometer’s numbers can’t be compared with it.
limits.brainGlucoseConstant: The brain uses about 4.4 g of sugar an hour here (about 106 g a day), the same all day: studies measured 100–145 g a day. Between meals the liver keeps it supplied, so no meal changes it.

card.title: Germ defence

barrier.title: Keeping germs out
barrier.text: Skin covers the body like a wall, and mucus in the nose traps germs. Stomach acid kills many germs, not all, so washing hands and clean water still matter.
barrier.picture: Germs stopped at the skin, and acid in the stomach.

cut.title: A cut lets germs in
cut.text: A cut or a thorn breaks the skin, and germs get in under it.
cut.picture: Germs getting in through a cut in the skin.

fight.title: White cells fight
fight.text: Blood brings white cells to the cut, which gets warm, red and swollen. Some white cells swallow germs and break them down. Lymph carries germs to the lymph nodes.
fight.picture: White cells round the cut, one swallowing a germ.

memory.title: Antibodies and memory
memory.text: In the lymph nodes, white cells make antibodies that fit this germ and stick to it. Some white cells remember it, so next time the body answers faster. Vaccines teach this memory without the illness.
memory.picture: Y-shaped antibodies stuck to germs, beside a lymph node.

card.cells: About 5,000–10,000 white cells per µL of blood (a µL is one millionth of a litre); labs differ.
card.source: Source: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, sections 18.4 (white cells) and 21.2 (stomach acid).

fluid.value: Lymph also takes about 3 L of tissue fluid a day back to the blood.
fluid.source: Source: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 21.1

road.why: They agree on the road. The book gives no amounts; the model’s come from a physiology textbook and from studies of blood fat after meals (OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §21.1; Nordestgaard 2016).

demo.title: Hot pan: reflex or thinking?
demo.lead: The same touch, twice, slowed down: the reflex through the spinal cord (●) and the route through the brain (○).
demo.picture: A hand touches a hot pan. A sensory neuron runs from the fingertip up the arm to the spinal cord; in the cord a relay neuron passes the signal to a motor neuron, which runs back to the arm muscle. The route through the brain goes up the spinal cord to the brain and back down.

steps.start: 0 ms: the fingertip touches the hot pan, and the heat receptor starts a signal.
steps.cord: {{ms}} ms: the signal reaches the spinal cord along the sensory neuron. A relay neuron passes it to the motor neuron; the route through the brain goes up the cord instead.
steps.reflex: {{ms}} ms: the arm muscle gets the signal and pulls the hand back.
steps.brain: {{ms}} ms: the command through the brain reaches the arm muscle.

demo.playing: The signals are on their way…
demo.result: The brain route takes about three times as long: {{brain}} ms against {{reflex}} ms.
demo.resultSlow: Without myelin even the reflex takes {{reflex}} ms, about {{times}} times as long as with it.
demo.myelinNote: A what-if: real motor nerves always have myelin. Without it, every nerve here would be as slow as a thin fibre with no myelin, about {{c}} m/s.
demo.slowed: Slowed down about {{times}} times: the counters show the real time.
demo.clock: The meal clock does not move this demo: nerves work in thousandths of a second.
demo.book: Book (NCERT Class 10, Ch 6, p. 102): reflex arcs evolved because “the thinking process of the brain is not fast enough”.
demo.limits: Model estimate: lengths of an average adult arm; heat goes in on a thin fibre with myelin at {{in}} m/s and the command comes out on a thick one at {{out}} m/s; each synapse takes {{synapse}} ms, and thinking adds {{thinking}} ms (from reaction-time studies). The clock stops when the muscle gets the signal: the skin's sensors and the muscle's own pull are left out. Children's arms are shorter, so their times are shorter.

cycle.title: Hormones over one cycle
cycle.lhWho: LH comes from the pituitary; estrogen and progesterone from the ovary.
cycle.alt: Estrogen rises to its highest around day 14, falls, then rises a little again around day 22. LH rises sharply to its highest on day 14 and is back down within a few days. Progesterone stays low until day 14, rises to its highest around day 22, and falls before the next cycle.
cycle.differ: Cycles differ: NCERT Class 9 says 21–35 days, often about 28. Menstruation usually lasts 3 to 7 days.
cycle.relative: Each line is drawn against its own highest level. The three are measured in different units, so compare when they rise and fall, not how tall the lines are.
cycle.clock: The meal clock does not move these panels.
cycle.study: The points are middle values from a study of 85 women (Anckaert and others, 2021), moved from their 29-day cycle (egg on day 15) to the book's 28 days (egg on day 14). The line between the points is drawn.
cycle.shareNote: Each number is a share of that hormone's own highest level.

flagship.title: One roti, one walk: what does every system do?

blood.question: Where is more blood going?
blood.book: NCERT Class 10: blood carries digested food around the body.
blood.model: While the intestine takes in food, more blood flows to it.

breaths.question: Why are breaths faster now?
breaths.book: Older NCERT Class 7 book (2024-25): 15–18 breaths a minute at rest.
breaths.model: Walking muscles use more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide, so breaths come faster and deeper: about 24 a minute instead of 16 without the walk.

sweat.question: Where does the extra heat go?
sweat.book: NCERT Class 6 (Curiosity, Ch 7, p. 128): the normal temperature of a healthy human body is taken to be 37.0 °C.
sweat.model: The walking muscles turn the extra energy into heat; sweat carries it away, so the body stays near 37 °C.

heart.question: Why does the heart beat faster now?
heart.book: Older NCERT Class 7 book (2024-25): 72–80 beats a minute at rest.
heart.model: The heart beats faster, about 94 a minute instead of 67 without the walk, to send more blood to the walking muscles.

water.question: Where did the water go?
water.book: NCERT Class 10: the kidneys filter about 180 L a day, and only a litre or two leaves as urine.
water.model: The kidneys send the extra water from the glass out as urine. Sweat took some water in the walk, so by now about 60 mL less has come out than without the walk.

fat.question: Did the roti raise blood fat?
fat.book: NCERT Class 10 (Ch 5, p. 94): lymph carries digested and absorbed fat from the intestine.
fat.model: Two rotis have only about 3 g of fat, so blood fat rises only a little: about 86 mg/dL at the most, from 80 before eating.
fat.insulin: Insulin rose as sugar from the roti reached the blood, to about 5 times its before-eating level at 1 h 25 min, and is falling back now.

why.title: Why does the model differ from the book?
why.exam: In the exam, write the book’s value.

where.book: the digested food is absorbed in the small intestine (NCERT Class 10, Ch 5, p. 98)
where.model: the small intestine takes in 97 % of the carbohydrate, 95 % of the protein and 95 % of the fat (textbook values)
where.why: They agree on where. The book gives no amounts; the model’s shares come from a physiology textbook and food tables (OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §23.7).

water.book: the wall of the large intestine absorbs more water from what is left (NCERT Class 10, Ch 5, p. 86)
water.model: the small intestine takes in 90 % of a meal’s water; the large intestine takes in 90 % of what reaches it (model estimate)
water.why: They agree. The small intestine’s 90 % is a textbook value; the large intestine’s share is this model’s own choice.

digestion.ask: The inside of the small intestine is covered in tiny finger-like villi. Why does that help it take in food?
